cards.front: How fast should you back up, and why?
cards.back: Reverse dulls control, so back slowly with a feathered or untouched pedal.

cards.front: Why crane your head past the headrest when backing?
cards.back: Crane your head past the headrest, since mirrors and cameras alone crop the view and warp depth.

cards.front: What is the backing posture?
cards.back: Twist hips around, drape the right arm over the seat, grip the wheel top left-handed, and sight over the right shoulder.

cards.front: What do you check before and during backing, and how do you move?
cards.back: Sweep behind and through blind zones before and during, then creep off the brake with gas only as needed.

cards.front: How do you steer when backing?
cards.back: Aim the wheel where you want the tail to go while watching travel through the rear side glass.
cards.memory_hook: Aim the tail, watch rear glass

cards.front: How do you back, and what beats mirrors and cameras?
cards.back: Backing crawls on a feathered pedal, while head turns beat mirrors and cameras.

cards.front: What does the backing posture involve, and what governs motion?
cards.back: The backing posture drapes an arm and sights over a shoulder, while checks and creep govern motion.

cards.front: How do you prepare a turn?
cards.back: Pre-pick your turn exit, bleed speed early, and scan for walkers and cars, shunning last-second sharp turns.

cards.front: Why hold your arc through a turn?
cards.back: Hold your arc: corner cutting and wide swings both invite crashes.

cards.front: How do planned turns differ from cut corners and wide swings?
cards.back: Planned turns pre-pick exits and bleed speed, while cut corners and wide swings invite crashes.

cards.front: When should you signal?
cards.back: Signal every lane change, turn, merge, and park to buy others reaction time, signaling even empty roads since blind zones may hide an audience.

cards.front: How far before a turn must you signal?
cards.back: Iowa demands signals one hundred feet before turns where limits run forty-five miles per hour or less, and three hundred feet where limits run faster.
cards.memory_hook: One hundred slow, three hundred fast

cards.front: When do you start and stop a turn signal?
cards.back: Blink before braking, yet past intervening streets, drives, and waiting entrants first, then kill the signal after turning.

cards.front: What earns a signal, and how do the distances differ?
cards.back: Every direction change earns a signal even on empty roads, while slow zones need one hundred feet and fast zones three hundred.
cards.memory_hook: Every change signals, feet by speed

cards.front: How do signals relate to braking and side streets?
cards.back: Signals precede braking yet follow side streets and waiting cars, while dead signals get cancelled.

cards.front: When do red lights allow a right turn?
cards.back: Red lights allow right turns after a full stop and full yield unless a no-turn-on-red sign forbids.

cards.front: When do red lights allow a left turn?
cards.back: Red lights allow left turns only from a one-way left lane onto another one-way street.
cards.memory_hook: Left on red: one-way to one-way

cards.front: How do rights and lefts on red differ?
cards.back: Rights on red need stops and yields short of bans, while lefts on red need one-way to one-way geometry.
cards.memory_hook: Rights stop and yield, lefts one-way

cards.front: When may you make a U-turn?
cards.back: U-turn only where unprohibited and safe.

cards.front: Why favor the next intersection over a three-point turn?
cards.back: Three-point turns court collisions, so favor the next intersection instead.

cards.front: How do U-turns and three-point turns compare?
cards.back: U-turns pass where legal and safe, while three-pointers lose to the next intersection.

cards.front: How do you make a lane move?
cards.back: Lane moves span lane swaps, ramp merges, and curb entries; shift one lane at a time into confirmed gaps while yielding to occupants.

cards.front: How do you announce and execute a lane move?
cards.back: Announce with signals and hold pace unless dropping to a slower lane, scanning throughout for surprises.

cards.front: What do you clear in the mirrors before a lane move?
cards.back: Clear rearview and side mirrors of target-lane cars and imminent passers.

cards.front: What does the shoulder check involve?
cards.back: Shoulder-check the move side for rear-corner lurkers while pinning the wheel straight against arm-follow reflex.

cards.front: Why scan the far lane before a lane move?
cards.back: Also scan the far lane for rivals diving at your same gap.

cards.front: How do lane moves shift, and what announces them?
cards.back: Lane moves shift singly into yielded gaps, while signals and steady pace announce them.

cards.front: What do mirrors clear, and what do shoulder checks do?
cards.back: Mirrors clear lanes and passers, while shoulder checks pin rear corners with a straight wheel.

cards.front: Why check the far lane before changing lanes?
cards.back: Before a lane change, check an additional lane farther over, if one exists: a driver there could be trying to enter the same lane you intend to use.

cards.front: When should you pass?
cards.back: Pass only where signs and markings bless it, room truly allows, and need demands.

cards.front: How many cars per pass, and which zones should you avoid?
cards.back: Take one car per pass and shun zones where cross traffic may pop from intersections and drives.

cards.front: How do you open a pass?
cards.back: Open a pass by confirming open lane ahead, clearing mirrors and blind zones, then signaling and accelerating in.

cards.front: When do you re-enter after a pass?
cards.back: Mid-pass watch fore, aft, and mirror, then re-enter gently once the passed nose shows in your mirror, cancel, and settle to safe speed.

cards.front: What do passes need, and what bounds them?
cards.back: Passes need permission, room, and need, while single victims and entry-free zones bound them.

cards.front: What do pass entries confirm, and what do exits await?
cards.back: Pass entries confirm space, mirrors, signals, and speed, while exits await mirror-visible noses and gentle returns.

cards.front: Which markings bless a pass?
cards.back: Broken white lines in your lane bless same-direction passes, while solid-and-broken yellow pairs bless only the dashed side.

cards.front: What does a double yellow center do, and what do yellow and white divide?
cards.back: Double yellow centers ban both directions, with yellow dividing foes and white dividing friends.

cards.front: How do the three center-line cases differ?
cards.back: Broken white blesses same-way passes and dashed yellow blesses its side, while double yellow bans all.
cards.memory_hook: Broken white, dashed yellow, double bans

cards.front: Where must you never pass because of sight?
cards.back: Never pass cresting hills or rounding blind curves.

cards.front: Within what distance of which places is passing banned?
cards.back: Never pass within one hundred feet of signed narrow bridges, viaducts, tunnels, railroad crossings, or intersections.
cards.memory_hook: No passing within one hundred feet

cards.front: Which two passes are banned outright?
cards.back: Never pass on the right nor into oncoming gaps too tight to survive.

cards.front: What blinds passes, and what bans them?
cards.back: Hills and curves blind passes, while hundred-foot zones, right sides, and tight gaps ban them.
